title: Natural Rights and the Social Contract
short: Hobbes argued people accept government to escape a "war of all against all"; Locke held that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property and may replace a government that violates them; Montesquieu urged separating powers.
trouble: Students credit Locke with "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness." Locke wrote of life, liberty and property (estate); "the pursuit of Happiness" is Jefferson's phrase in the Declaration.

blocks.html: Why should anyone obey a government at all? Three European writers gave answers the American founders read closely. Each starts by imagining a state of nature, life with no government, and asks what people would agree to in order to leave it. That agreement is the social contract. It builds on the forms of government you just met.

doc.title: Three thinkers in their own words
doc.source: Hobbes, Leviathan, ch. 13 (1651); Locke, Second Treatise, §87 (1764 ed.); Montesquieu, The Spirit of Laws, Book XI, ch. 6 (Nugent tr., 1758)
paras: Hobbes: "...during the time men live without a common Power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition which is called Warre; and such a warre, as is of every man, against every man."
Locke: Man "hath by nature a power, not only to preserve his property, that is, his life, liberty and estate, against the injuries and attempts of other men..."
Montesquieu: "Again, there is no liberty, if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers."

marks.note: Without government, Hobbes says, everyone is at risk from everyone.

marks.text: power of judging be not separated
marks.note: The root of separation of powers.

blocks.html: The thinkers start from the same picture but reach different ends. Hobbes thought the state of nature was so dangerous that people should give a sovereign nearly unlimited power. Locke thought people keep their natural rights when they form a government, so a government that violates them breaks the contract, and the people may "alter or abolish" it, as the Declaration later put it. Montesquieu supplied the design: split power so no one can abuse all of it. The American system took Locke's purpose and Montesquieu's design.

Social contract theory says legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed. Locke: government exists to protect natural rights to life, liberty and property. Montesquieu: separate the powers to protect liberty.

blocks.title: Who said it?
blocks.q: "Life, liberty and estate": whose idea, and where does a similar phrase appear in American founding documents?
steps: "Estate" is an old word for property; the phrase is Locke's, in the Second Treatise.
Jefferson's Declaration (1776) lists "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness," changing the third item.
blocks.a: John Locke; the Declaration echoes it with "the pursuit of Happiness."

blocks.title: Tracing an idea into the Constitution
blocks.q: Which thinker's idea explains why the Constitution puts lawmaking, enforcing and judging in three separate articles?
steps: Articles I, II and III create a Congress, a President and courts.
Splitting those three powers is Montesquieu's rule for keeping liberty.

blocks.html: Crediting Locke with "the pursuit of happiness." Locke wrote of life, liberty and estate (property); "the pursuit of Happiness" is Jefferson's phrase. Check: if a question quotes the Declaration, the author is Jefferson; if it says "estate" or "property," it is Locke.
